title: Beat Postcard
user: Two friends who want to trade short, playable rhythm challenges in a browser without copyrighted song libraries, installs, or competitive rank pressure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An HN player likes the auto-charting idea but reports that the basic tempo-input flow does not work in practice, showing both desire for browser rhythm play and sensitivity to input onboarding.
The fetched Chrome Web Store page is the live DanceJump-for-YouTube rhythm-game distribution page; its YouTube dependency highlights the licensing/platform risk to avoid.

recurrence: The feedback names a concrete browser rhythm-game interaction people wanted to use but could not successfully start; web rhythm games repeatedly surface in 2026 HN search results.
current_workaround: Install a desktop rhythm game, use a YouTube extension, or share a recording rather than a playable challenge.
incumbents_and_gap: osu! and browser auto-charters offer deep or copyright-dependent music play. They do not provide a tiny legal, link-shareable asynchronous duet based on built-in percussion.
smallest_useful_product: A 45-second call-and-response game: make an eight-beat pattern from original synthesized kit sounds, send a link, and the recipient mirrors it then adds one bar. Runs differ through generated tempo, accents, and reply choices. Non-goals: song uploads, YouTube integration, ranked ladders, or MIDI hardware support.
success_measure: At least 25% of first completed patterns receive a reply, and median first-play calibration completes in under 20 seconds.
monetization: free — the compact share loop benefits from universal access; a one-time sound-pack purchase is optional later.
constraints: Use original synthesized samples only; schedule with Web Audio rather than network timing; provide keyboard, touch, and reduced-flash modes; no biometric rhythm profiling.
why_distinct: It is social musical call-and-response with original audio, not another copyrighted-song chart player.
